netmix_long <- netmix_candidates[[which.max(netmix_elbo)]]

We fix KK, the number of roles, at two in advance so the classroom result remains easy to inspect. NetMix then learns what those two role patterns look like. The nine best runs recover essentially the same role-to-role probabilities after matching the otherwise arbitrary role labels. The other runs stop at clearly worse approximate fit scores. The result therefore does not look like an accident of one starting value. This check applies only to the chosen two-role model; it does not show that two is the correct number of roles.

The argument n.hmmstates = 1 is easy to misread. In NetMix, one hidden state means there is no hidden Markov model. The fit estimates a separate membership vector for every state-year and shares one role matrix across years, but it does not estimate transition probabilities or smooth a state’s memberships over time. The full NetMix framework can fit those dynamics; this fast classroom specification does not.

15.2 How the Fast NetMix Estimator Works

NetMix begins with rough guesses about each state-year’s two role weights. Using those guesses, it estimates the four probabilities in the role matrix. It then asks whether each state-year’s observed source and target relationships look more like one template or the other and updates its weights. The new weights produce a new role matrix, so the program goes back and forth until another round barely improves the approximate fit.

The evidence lower bound, or ELBO, is the score used to decide whether the approximation is still improving. A larger ELBO is better for runs of the same specification. It is not a probability, a goodness-of-fit test, or proof that two roles are correct.

This 18-state system is small enough that full-batch updates are faster and more stable than stochastic subsampling. NetMix also offers stochastic variational inference for larger networks, where each iteration updates only a sample of nodes. Both routes are approximate and can settle at local optima, so multiple starts, role-label alignment, and calibration remain necessary. hessian = FALSE keeps this a descriptive point fit without standard errors.

c(converged = netmix_long$converged, iterations = netmix_long$niter, final_elbo = netmix_long$LowerBound)
#>  converged iterations final_elbo 
#>     1.0000   100.0000  -234.6401

15.3 Read the Block Matrix Before Naming the Roles

netmix_theta_raw <- plogis(netmix_long$BlockModel)
active_role <- which.max(rowMeans(netmix_theta_raw) + colMeans(netmix_theta_raw))
quiet_role <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(netmix_theta_raw)), active_role)
netmix_role_order <- c(quiet_role, active_role)
netmix_theta <- netmix_theta_raw[netmix_role_order, netmix_role_order, drop = FALSE]
dimnames(netmix_theta) <- list(source_role = c("lower involvement", "broad event involvement"), target_role = c("lower involvement", "broad event involvement"))
round(netmix_theta, 2)
#>                          target_role
#> source_role               lower involvement broad event involvement
#>   lower involvement                    0.05                    0.83
#>   broad event involvement              0.86                    0.97

Read rows as source roles and columns as target roles. For hypothetical state-years that fully match the lower-involvement role, the fitted probability is about 0.05. It is about 0.83 or 0.86 when one side fully matches each role, and about 0.97 when both sides fully match the broadly involved role. Actual state-years usually mix the two roles, so their fitted dyad-year probability averages all four cells using their role weights.

15.4 Compare Annual Membership Profiles With Observed Breadth

membership_long <- data.frame(key = colnames(netmix_long$MixedMembership), t(netmix_long$MixedMembership), check.names = FALSE)
names(membership_long)[-1] <- paste0("Group ", seq_len(netmix_long$n_blocks))
membership_long$state <- sub("@[0-9]+$", "", membership_long$key)
membership_long$year <- as.integer(sub("^.*@", "", membership_long$key))
membership_long$broad_role_membership <- membership_long[[paste0("Group ", active_role)]]
source_breadth <- aggregate(high_event_volume ~ source + year, netmix_dyad, mean)
names(source_breadth) <- c("state", "year", "source_breadth")
target_breadth <- aggregate(high_event_volume ~ target + year, netmix_dyad, mean)
names(target_breadth) <- c("state", "year", "target_breadth")
membership_long <- merge(membership_long, source_breadth, by = c("state", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
membership_long <- merge(membership_long, target_breadth, by = c("state", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
membership_long$observed_breadth <- (membership_long$source_breadth + membership_long$target_breadth) / 2
membership_breadth_correlations <- c(
  source = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$source_breadth),
  target = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$target_breadth),
  combined = cor(membership_long$broad_role_membership, membership_long$observed_breadth)
)
round(membership_breadth_correlations, 3)
#>   source   target combined 
#>    0.923    0.921    0.953
focus_states <- c("Syrian Arab Republic", "Russian Federation", "Iran, Islamic Republic Of", "Pakistan", "United States", "Israel")
profile_long <- melt(membership_long[membership_long$state %in% focus_states, ], id.vars = c("state", "year"), measure.vars = c("broad_role_membership", "observed_breadth"), variable.name = "measure", value.name = "value")
profile_long$state_label <- factor(profile_long$state, levels = focus_states, labels = c("Syria", "Russia", "Iran", "Pakistan", "United States", "Israel"))
profile_long$measure <- factor(profile_long$measure, levels = c("broad_role_membership", "observed_breadth"), labels = c("NetMix role weight", "Observed breadth"))
ggplot(profile_long, aes(year, value, color = measure, linetype = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ state_label) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#18453B", "#7BBD00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Annual relational profile", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The broad-role weight correlates about 0.95 with a simple observed quantity: the share of possible source-side and target-side relationships that cross the threshold. In this application, the role mostly summarizes how widely a state appears in high-volume coded relationships during a year. It is not a hidden ideological, alliance, or geopolitical camp.

The United States remains strongly associated with broad involvement throughout the panel. Syria’s annual membership is near zero through 2010, rises in 2011, reaches about 0.37 in 2012, and remains elevated through 2014 as the number of selected states connected to it by above-threshold relationships widens. These annual estimates line up with recognizable historical periods, but they are not a learned transition path or an explanation of the Syrian civil war. System-wide density shifts and ICEWS coverage can also move the profiles because this role-only model has no year intercept.

15.5 Does the Model Put the More Active Relationships Near the Top?

netmix_mm <- t(netmix_long$MixedMembership)
netmix_dd <- netmix_long$dyadic.data
sender_key <- paste(netmix_dd[["(sid)"]], netmix_dd[["(tid)"]], sep = "@")
receiver_key <- paste(netmix_dd[["(rid)"]], netmix_dd[["(tid)"]], sep = "@")
sender_mm <- netmix_mm[match(sender_key, rownames(netmix_mm)), , drop = FALSE]
receiver_mm <- netmix_mm[match(receiver_key, rownames(netmix_mm)), , drop = FALSE]
netmix_pred <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(netmix_dd)), function(ii) sum(outer(sender_mm[ii, ], receiver_mm[ii, ]) * netmix_theta_raw), numeric(1))
calibration <- data.frame(observed = netmix_long$Y, predicted = netmix_pred)
calibration$bin <- cut(calibration$predicted, quantile(calibration$predicted, probs = seq(0, 1, .2), na.rm = TRUE), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("lowest", "second", "third", "fourth", "highest"))
aggregate(cbind(observed, predicted) ~ bin, calibration, mean)
bin observed predicted
lowest 0.0138191 0.0784206
second 0.0742138 0.0962294
third 0.1469849 0.1482782
fourth 0.2402516 0.2315161
highest 0.6143216 0.5679937 
brier_model <- mean((calibration$observed - calibration$predicted)^2)
brier_null <- mean((calibration$observed - mean(calibration$observed))^2)
round(c(role_model = brier_model, constant_probability = brier_null), 3)
#>           role_model constant_probability 
#>                0.115                0.170

The model gives every ordered state pair in every year a predicted chance of crossing the 20-event threshold. We line up those cases from the smallest predicted chance to the largest and split the line into five equally sized groups. If the model is separating relatively quiet relationships from more active ones, the cases near the top should cross the threshold much more often than the cases near the bottom. That is what we see. Only about 1 out of every 100 cases in the bottom group crosses the threshold, compared with 61 out of every 100 in the top group.

We can also ask whether the probabilities themselves are about right. For the bottom group, the model predicts 8 out of 100, but only 1 out of 100 crosses the threshold. For the middle group, it predicts 15 and we observe 15. For the top group, it predicts 57 and we observe 61. The model therefore does a useful job of putting the more active relationships near the top, but it overstates the chance for the quietest cases. The Brier score is the average squared gap between each predicted probability and its zero-or-one outcome, so lower is better: 0.115 for NetMix versus 0.17 for giving every case the same probability. We learned and checked the model on the same observations, so this is a description of how well it reconstructs this panel. It is not a test of how well it would forecast a new year.

WarningWhat We Can and Cannot Claim

Within this chosen two-role model, we can describe how each state-year’s relationship pattern resembles the two roles. We cannot treat those roles as natural geopolitical kinds, read a role weight as the probability that a state is “in conflict,” claim that the model estimated transitions, compare role numbers across separate fits without matching them, or generalize from this selected event-rich case set to all states. A paper should compare thresholds, actor sets, role counts, hidden-state structures, starting values, and predictor specifications, then evaluate held-out dyads or years before making predictive claims.

16 How the Three Representations Handle the Missing Pattern

Representation Latent quantity Best at Main limitation
Social relations model (SRM) One activity score per actor, or separate source-side and target-side scores Recurring broad actor involvement and reciprocity Cannot represent special affinity among particular groups of actors
Stochastic blockmodel (SBM) One discrete relational role per actor A readable role-to-role cooperation pattern Actors in one role are treated as interchangeable unless the model is extended
Repeated-network mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel, fitted with NetMix A separate blend of roles for every actor-year, with one shared role matrix Comparing how annual relationship patterns differ With one hidden state, it has no transition process or smoothing across years

17 What Did the Models Show?

17.1 Cooperation Among Armed Organizations in Syria

These data record claimed joint operations among armed opposition organizations in Syria from July 2012 through June 2015. Two findings stand out. First, organizations closer to one another in estimated size tended to carry out more joint operations together. Second, some organizations took part in joint operations with far more partners than their measured ideology, size, location, and sponsorship would lead us to expect.

Al-Nusrah Front (ANF) and Ahrar al-Sham Islamic Movement (ASIM) stand out most clearly. They carried out an operation together, and each also carried out operations with many organizations that seldom worked with one another. The blockmodel summarizes this as a two-organization core connected to a much larger set of organizations with few ties among themselves. That is a description of the cooperation network. It does not mean ANF and ASIM had the same goals or formed one lasting coalition.

17.2 Conflictual Events Among States

Here one case is an ordered pair of states in one year. The outcome equals one when ICEWS records more than 20 materially conflictual events directed from the first state toward the second. It does not indicate whether a war occurred or how severe the conflict was.

After accounting for the year and for each state’s recurring place on both sides of these relationships, pairs in the same region crossed the threshold more often than pairs in different regions. Pairs with larger Polity-score differences also crossed it more often. These are adjusted comparisons within this dataset, not evidence that moving a state to another region or changing its regime score would cause more events.

The United States appeared in many above-threshold relationships in both directions throughout 2002 to 2014. Syria appeared in relatively few through 2010. After 2011, Syria appeared in many more, especially as the state toward which events were directed. The bootstrap intervals show that this change is large relative to the uncertainty in the fitted model.

NetMix describes the same panel in a simpler way. For each state and year, it asks whether the list of above-threshold partners was short or broad. The United States had a broad list throughout the panel. Syria’s list broadened sharply after 2011. NetMix is not identifying a geopolitical camp or estimating a fixed sequence through which states move.

ICEWS is built from events coded from news reports. The patterns can reflect state behavior, what news sources covered, and how the events were coded. They do not measure battlefield severity and they do not establish that region or regime difference caused the events.

18 Exercises

  1. Inference: Let β=0.5\beta=0.5, γ=1\gamma=1, and z=αx+ez=\alpha x+e, where ee contains recurring actor effects. Compute the naive target when α=0.4\alpha=0.4, −0.4-0.4, and 00. Explain why the zero-correlation case can still have incorrect independent-row uncertainty.
  2. SRM: Inspect the eight largest and smallest gade_srm$APM values. Choose two organizations and write an interpretation that does not turn the latent effect into a fixed trait.
  3. SRM Fit: Explain in one sentence what the posterior predictive check reproduces and what third-order pattern it misses.
  4. Blocks: Use the observed numerators and denominators to explain why the cross-cell evidence is stronger than the fitted core-core probability. Then compare the two- and three-block solutions.
  5. Longitudinal SRM: Choose one state and compare its source-side and target-side paths. Identify a change that is clear relative to its bootstrap interval and one that is not.
  6. NetMix: Compare raw source-side breadth, target-side breadth, and fitted membership for Syria, Russia, Iran, and the United States. Explain what the role adds without calling it a transition process or a geopolitical bloc.

19 Reading

  • Back and Kenny (2010), “The Social Relations Model: How to Understand Dyadic Processes,” for the core actor, partner, and relationship decomposition.
  • Hoff (2005), “Bilinear Mixed-Effects Models for Dyadic Data,” for the additive social-relations regression framework introduced here. Day 10 adds the multiplicative term.
  • Gade, Gabbay, Hafez, and Kelly (2019), “Networks of Cooperation: Rebel Alliances in Fragmented Civil Wars,” for the Syrian cooperation application used here.
  • Minhas et al. (2022), “Taking Dyads Seriously,” for the simulation evidence, applied reanalyses, latent-effect interpretation, and the correlated-omitted-variable limitation.
  • Holland, Laskey, and Leinhardt (1983), “Stochastic Blockmodels: First Steps,” for the generative blockmodel.
  • Karrer and Newman (2011), “Stochastic Blockmodels and Community Structure in Networks,” for degree-corrected blocks.
  • Boschee et al. (2015), “ICEWS Coded Event Data,” for the source-target event records used in the longitudinal classroom panel.
  • Olivella, Pratt, and Imai (2022), “Dynamic Stochastic Blockmodel Regression for Network Data,” for the broader dynamic mixed-membership framework and international-conflict application behind NetMix. Our one-hidden-state classroom fit deliberately does not estimate its HMM transition layer.

The Linux binary is the least portable option because it must match the system architecture and a compatible R setup. On Linux or WSL, installing `build-essential` and using the GitHub source route is usually more reliable.
